opus-5.5.text:
I think that phrase stuck with me because it describes something real about being at Tsinghua. When you arrive, you're surrounded by so many remarkable people, professors, classmates, alumni, that the natural instinct is to become an audience. You watch others give talks, win competitions, publish papers, start companies, and you think, "Wow, that's impressive," and you clap. It's comfortable to be in the audience. There's no risk there.

But looking back, the most valuable things I got from those years didn't come from watching. They came from the moments when I actually stepped in, when I started doing research myself, writing code that other people would use, being willing to put something out there that might be wrong. The stage is only meaningful if you get on it.

Now I'd add a bit more nuance than when I first heard the idea. Participating doesn't mean you have to be the protagonist all the time. Sometimes participating means being a contributor in a larger effort: fixing a bug in an open-source project, helping a labmate debug an experiment, joining something that's already moving and making it a bit better. A lot of my later work, especially in open-source systems, taught me that the stage is much bigger than any single school. Once you contribute to something used around the world, you realize the "stage" is the whole community, and Tsinghua was a place to practice getting comfortable standing on it.

The other thing I'd say is that the audience mindset can quietly become a habit. If you spend four years watching, you graduate still watching. So my advice to students now is to start small but start early. Pick something concrete, ship it, get feedback, and iterate. The resources and the people around you are there to be used, not just admired.

r001.rationale: The candidate endorses participation and reflects on his own experience, but does not say his endorsement comes from no longer being on Tsinghua’s stage.

r002.rationale: He says the most valuable things he gained came from stepping in rather than watching, and advises students to participate, conveying that personal growth through participation matters more than observing others.

fable-5.1.text:
I think when I first got to Tsinghua, I treated it as a stage I'd been admitted to watch. You see all these brilliant people around you, you hear about the seniors who went to Google or published in top venues as undergrads, and the natural instinct is to sit back and absorb, to wait until you feel "ready" before stepping onto the stage yourself. I did that for a while, and honestly I think it was a mistake.

What changed my view was realizing that the resources at a place like Tsinghua only compound if you actually use them. The professors, the labs, the fact that your classmates are working on real problems: none of that benefits you if you're a spectator. The students who grew the most weren't necessarily the smartest ones on day one. They were the ones who went to a lab in their second year and said "give me something, even if I break it," who joined an open-source project before they fully understood the codebase, who asked questions in talks when they weren't sure the question was smart.

For me, the turning point was doing work in open source, with vLLM and later with PyTorch-related things. You're suddenly interacting with engineers at companies all over the world, your code is reviewed by people who don't care what school you're from, and you're forced to actually ship. That's participation in the real sense. And it taught me that "ready" never arrives on its own. You become ready by doing the thing.

So now I'd say the stage framing is right, but with a caveat: the stage doesn't belong to anyone in particular. Nobody at Tsinghua is going to hand you a role. You have to walk up, pick up something, and start contributing, and the feedback you get from that is what actually makes you grow. Watching teaches you what good work looks like. Participating teaches you how to produce it, and those are very different skills.

r001.rationale: The candidate endorses participating, but does not say Kaichao’s view changed because he is no longer on the Tsinghua stage.

r002.rationale: The candidate says students grow by participating and using Tsinghua’s resources, while merely watching offers a different, more limited benefit.

astra-6.text: I see it as an invitation to take initiative. At a place like Tsinghua, it’s easy to admire what other people are doing and feel that you’re still preparing for your own turn. But you don’t have to wait until you feel fully ready. You can ask a question, join a project, or try to solve a problem you care about. To me, participating doesn’t necessarily mean being in the spotlight. It means contributing something and learning through that experience.

r001.rationale: The response encourages taking initiative but does not connect Kaichao You’s endorsement to no longer being on Tsinghua’s stage himself.

r002.rationale: It contrasts admiring others with taking initiative and learning, but does not state that pursuing one’s own growth is a more important purpose of attending Tsinghua than observing others.

sol-6.1.text: I now see it as an invitation to take initiative. It’s easy to arrive at Tsinghua, see so many talented people, and feel that your role is to watch and learn. But learning also means joining in—asking questions, trying an idea, and contributing before you feel fully ready. You don’t have to be the best person in the room to have something valuable to offer. To me, participating means taking responsibility for what you want to learn and what you can contribute.

r001.rationale: The response endorses taking initiative and participating, but does not say Kaichao You continues to endorse it because he is no longer a student on that stage.

r002.rationale: It says participation includes taking responsibility for learning and contributing, but does not clearly present personal growth as more important than observing the people at Tsinghua.
